To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the use of a [Ru(bpy2]2+ 90° accepter tecton in coordination-driven self assembly results in emergent photophysical properties in the M6L4 cages, including increased visible-light absorption, a biexponential decay in the emission band, and a shift in the reduction potential relative to the parent complex [Ru(bpy3]Cl2.

we report the use of a [Ru(bpy)]2+ tecton in coordination-driven self assembly to synthesize a metallacycle and a truncated tetrahedral metal cage that possesses emergent photophysical and electrochemical properties.

coordination-driven self- assembly of [Ru(bppy)2]2+, a 90° tecton, with 2,4',6-tris(3-pyridyl)1,3, 5-triazine (L) and 4,4' bipyridine (L) results in a truncated tetrahedral M6L4 and a M4L6 metallacycle.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the synthesis of new molecular materials that exhibit unique photophysical properties that are not observed for their individual components.
the use of coordination-driven self- assembly to create new architectures that exhibit unique electronic and photophysical properties.
the design of coordination-driven self-assemblies that exhibit novel properties arising from the unique electronic structure of the resulting supramolecular structures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the coordination-driven self- assembly of ruthenium polypyriydyl nodes results in emergent photophysical and electrochemical properties that are attributed to the unique electronic structure of the resulting cage molecule.
the coordination-driven self-association of ruthenium polypyrides results in a new class of molecules with emergent photophysical and electronic properties.

the coordination-driven self-organization of ruthenium polypyriyl nodes results in emergent photophysical and electrochemical properties that can be attributed to the electronic structure of the assembled cage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

coordination-driven self- assembly is an effective method to synthesize new metallosupramolecular species with unique photophysical and electrochemical properties that are not found in the parent complexes.

the use of the M fragment allows for a unique electronic structure to be achieved, resulting in emergent properties that are distinct from those of [Ru(byp)3]Cl and other ruthenium polypyrridyl complexes.
we have demonstrated that a coordination-driven self- assembly approach can be used to synthesize a metallo cage with emergent photophysical and electrochemical properties.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the electronic structure of the cage molecule is a combination of the electronic structure of its building blocks and that it can be tuned by the choice of building blocks.
the electronic properties of the cage are dictated by the electronic structure of the M4L4 building block and not by the M6L4 topology.
the use of a metal fragment as a 180° donor tecton in coordination-driven self-assemblies can lead to the formation of discrete architectures with emergent properties.
